opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Looking back, my approach has shifted from pure modeling toward thinking about the algorithm and the hardware together.

When I started, the main question in linear attention was expressiveness: how do we close the quality gap with softmax attention? Most work focused on the feature map, finding a better kernel to approximate softmax. Over time I became convinced that was the wrong framing. Linear attention isn't a cheap approximation of softmax attention. It's a recurrent model with a matrix-valued hidden state, and the real question is how you *update* that state.

Seen that way, the design space looks different. The first big lever is gating, or forgetting. Vanilla linear attention just keeps adding key-value outer products into the state, so it gets cluttered and can't discard anything. Adding data-dependent decay, as in gated linear attention and related models like Mamba-style selective state spaces, gives the model a way to forget, and that helps a lot in practice.

The second lever is the update rule itself. Purely additive updates can't really overwrite stored associations. The delta rule changes that. You treat the state as a key-value memory and do something like an online regression step: retrieve what's currently stored for a key, compare it with the new value, and correct the error. That's DeltaNet, and combining it with gating, as in Gated DeltaNet, gave clear improvements on associative recall and retrieval tasks, where linear models were traditionally weakest. Framing the update as an optimization step on a test-time objective also connects nicely to the broader "test-time training" view, which suggests richer updates and objectives worth exploring.

The other half of my thinking, and it's become just as important, is efficiency on real hardware. A model with linear complexity on paper can be slower than FlashAttention if it isn't parallelizable and doesn't use tensor cores. So a lot of my work went into chunkwise parallel algorithms: within a chunk you use matmul-heavy parallel computation, and across chunks you pass the recurrent state. For the delta rule this was nontrivial, since the naive recurrence looks inherently sequential. Using things like the WY representation for products of Householder-like matrices let us train it in parallel efficiently. That's also why we built the flash-linear-attention library: good ideas need fast, reusable kernels or nobody adopts them.

More recently I've been less dogmatic about pure linear models. Hybrids that mix a few full attention layers with mostly linear or recurrent layers seem like a very practical sweet spot. The linear layers handle cheap long-range compression, and the occasional attention layer provides precise retrieval. So the evolution has been from "approximate softmax" to "design a better recurrent memory update," always with an eye on whether it actually runs fast on GPUs, and then on how these pieces fit together in a full architecture.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd say my approach has gone through roughly three phases, and each one came from realizing I'd been optimizing the wrong thing.

The first phase was about compute. When I started working on linear attention, the dominant question was expressivity on paper versus actual throughput on a GPU. A lot of early linear attention papers looked great in FLOP counts but were slower than FlashAttention in practice, because the recurrent form is memory-bound and the parallel form didn't map well onto tensor cores. So my early work, things like the chunkwise formulation in Gated Linear Attention and the flash-linear-attention library, was really about asking: can we write kernels where the chunk-level computation is dense matrix multiplies, so we actually get hardware efficiency? I think that mattered a lot, because it made the whole research direction credible. People stopped asking whether linear attention could be fast and started asking whether it could be good.

The second phase was about the recurrence itself. Once speed wasn't the bottleneck, it became clear that the plain additive update, where you just accumulate outer products of keys and values into a matrix, is a very weak memory. It has no way to forget, and it has no way to correct an association once it's written. Gating gave you forgetting, which is where GLA, Mamba2, RetNet and so on converged. But forgetting is a blunt instrument. It decays everything uniformly, or at best per-channel. The DeltaNet line of thinking was the shift for me: treat the state as something you're doing online learning on. The delta rule is literally one step of gradient descent on a reconstruction loss for the key-value association. That reframing meant the recurrence has a key-dependent transition, so you can selectively erase what was stored under a particular key and replace it. Gated DeltaNet combined that with the gating, and that combination turned out to be where a lot of the gains in things like in-context retrieval and state tracking came from. The challenge was again hardware: the delta rule introduces a dependency chain within a chunk, so we had to find a WY-style representation to keep it parallelizable.

The third phase, which is where I am now, is about asking what the right optimizer is for that fast-weight view. If the delta rule is one gradient step, then you can ask about momentum, about higher-order structure, about whether the transition should be a rank-one Householder-like update or something richer, like products of them, which gets you toward more expressive state-tracking capabilities that diagonal or scalar-gated models provably can't do. I also think more carefully now about the interplay between layers, like mixing a few softmax attention layers with linear layers, rather than insisting on purity. For a long time I think the field, myself included, treated "fully linear" as the goal. I've come to see it as a design space, where the question is what the recurrent layers are good at, what global attention is good at, and how little of the expensive thing you need.

If I had to summarize the evolution, it's that I moved from "make the kernel fast" to "make the memory smarter" to "think of the whole thing as a learning algorithm running inside the forward pass, and make sure every step of that algorithm still maps onto hardware." Those three constraints have to be satisfied at once, and the interesting ideas tend to be the ones that sit right at the intersection.

astra-6.text:
I’d frame the evolution as moving from improving an individual mechanism to thinking about the whole architecture. With linear attention, it’s tempting to focus on efficiency: can we make the computation cheaper or the state smaller? But the more important question is what information the model can retain and how effectively it can use that information later.

So my emphasis has shifted toward understanding the trade-offs between efficiency, expressiveness, and trainability. If a model struggles, is the limitation in the memory update, the way it retrieves information, or the way the architecture is trained? Those questions lead to more targeted changes than simply adding complexity.

And ultimately, I think the improvements have to hold up in practice. A better theoretical complexity is valuable, but you also want good hardware utilization, stable training, and strong performance at a comparable compute budget. That makes architecture design much more of a joint problem than optimizing the attention mechanism alone.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d frame the evolution as moving from individual architectural changes toward understanding the whole system. With linear attention, the question is not just how to make attention cheaper, but how to preserve useful information as the sequence grows. That means thinking about what the state stores, how it gets updated, and what the model can retrieve from it.

And then there’s the practical side: an idea has to train well and run efficiently. So the approach becomes a loop between understanding the mechanism, testing the quality, and checking whether the implementation actually delivers the efficiency you wanted.
